sentences.text: The skull of Rhabdognathus keiniensis measured 73.1 centimeters in total length, with an extremely elongated snout comprising approximately 75% of that distance.
Its mandible was as high as it was wide or even taller, a trait distinguishing it from Hyposaurus, and featured an extremely long mandibular symphysis extending past the nineteenth tooth socket.
The genus was named by Swinton in 1930 based on a lower jaw fragment found in Nigeria.

Specimens dating back to the Maastrichtian era were identified in 2008, while two skulls originally assigned to the group were later reclassified as new species, R. aslerensis and R. keiniensis, both found in Mali.
Stéphane Jouve assessed the type species R. rarus as dubious because it was indeterminate at the species level.
The species Rhabdognathus compressus was reassigned to the genus Congosaurus after analysis showed its lower jaw was more similar to Congosaurus bequaerti.
Rhabdognathus is believed to be the closest relative to the extinct genus Atlantosuchus.
Fossils are known from rocks of the Paleocene epoch in western Africa, though the animal lived from the Maastrichtian to the Thanetian, between 72.2 and 56 million years ago.
